text: It is very seldom that ordinary people like John and myself secure an old colonial mansion for the summer, so I cannot help feeling that something is strange about the place. <break time="0.8s" /> John, who is a practical physician, laughs at me when I say so, but one expects that in marriage, and he has no patience with anything that cannot be seen or measured. <break time="0.8s" /> If a physician of high standing, who is also ones own husband, assures everyone that there is nothing really the matter with one except a temporary nervous depression, what is one to do. <break time="0.8s" /> So I take phosphates and tonics, breathe fresh air, and am absolutely forbidden to work until I am well again, although I personally believe that congenial work would do me good. <break time="0.8s" /> I write this journal in secret, hiding it whenever John comes near, for it exhausts me a good deal to be so sly about it or else to meet heavy opposition. <break time="0.8s" /> The house stands quite alone, well back from the road, three miles from the village, and it is surrounded by hedges and walls and gates that lock. <break time="0.8s" /> I wanted a room downstairs that opened onto the piazza and had roses all over the window, but John would not hear of it. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead, he chose the big airy nursery at the top of the house, where the windows are barred for little children and there are rings and things in the walls.
